docs.D01_macro_context.md:
Title: Disinflation, continued growth and restrictive policy
Source: compiled from: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_07122023.pdf; https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/publications/bea/newsreleases/bea_newsreleases_23-34_20230728.pdf; https://www.bea.gov/sites/default/files/2023-07/gdp2q23_adv.pdf; https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20230726a.htm
Date: 2023-07-28

The July 12 CPI release reports June headline inflation of 3.0% year over year and core inflation of 4.8%. Monthly headline and core increases were both 0.2%. Inflation had moderated, but the core rate remained above the Federal Reserve's objective.

The July 28 personal-income/outlays release reports June PCE inflation of 3.0% year over year and core PCE inflation of 4.1%. CPI and PCE use different coverage and weights; they are not interchangeable series.

These observations support disinflation and continued underlying price pressure at the same time. Neither a permanent return to 2% nor a permanently higher inflation regime follows mechanically from one month's data.

The July 27 advance GDP release reports real growth of 2.4% annualized in Q2, following 2.0% in Q1 on that release's vintage. These are the estimates then available, not later revised figures.

On July 26, the FOMC raised the federal-funds target range to 5.25%-5.50%. It said inflation remained elevated and that it would assess additional information, cumulative tightening and policy lags in determining the appropriate stance.

The short policy rate and the 30-year yield answer different questions. The latter reflects expected future short rates, inflation, real rates and term/risk compensation over a much longer horizon. A high current fed-funds rate does not prove that long yields must rise.

The long-rate risk case is that inflation settles above the market's implicit path, fiscal demand remains strong or term premium rises. The bond-supportive case is that disinflation persists and restrictive policy eventually slows growth.

No July CPI release published in August, later payroll revisions, October yield peak or geopolitical event is included. The information set ends with August 2 market/supply information in other documents.

The hedge question is therefore probabilistic and price-dependent. The economy has not shown the immediate contraction feared by some investors, yet monetary policy is restrictive and lagged effects remain uncertain. A defensible position must relate this range of outcomes to long-duration portfolio risk and actual option terms rather than simply extrapolate the latest inflation print.
docs.D02_market_pricing.md:
Title: The long curve at the cutoff
Source: compiled from: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/DGS10; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/DGS30; https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20230726a.htm
Date: 2023-08-02

Federal Reserve H.15 constant-maturity data show a 10-year Treasury yield of 4.08% and 30-year yield of 4.17% on August 2. These are daily benchmark yield observations, not the execution price or strike of a particular derivative.

The 30-year series was 4.02% on July 31 and 4.11% on August 1. It had already risen 15bp over those two sessions by the cutoff. The pack uses only historical rows through August 2 from the modern database and excludes later observations.

The policy target range is 5.25%-5.50%, above both long-maturity yields. The curve therefore does not simply project the current policy rate unchanged for thirty years. Expected normalization and term compensation matter.

The 30-year nominal yield is not a market inflation forecast. It combines real yields, expected inflation and risk/term premia. No dated TIPS breakeven series or model term-premium estimate was independently recovered, so the pack does not invent a precise decomposition.

A long-duration bond has substantial price sensitivity to yield changes. The sensitivity varies by coupon, maturity and price; constant-maturity yield data do not identify a single bond's exact duration or convexity.

Likewise, payer-swaption pricing depends on the underlying swap rate, strike, expiry, tenor and implied volatility. A Treasury benchmark yield is relevant context but not a complete option-price input, and swap/Treasury basis can move.

An exact executable options surface, premium, notional, dealer bid/ask and funding/collateral terms were not recovered. There is no numeric claim that an unspecified structure offers a particular payoff multiple or limited premium percentage.

The observed yield provides a starting point for scenario analysis: further inflation/rate repricing could hurt long bonds and equity duration, while disinflation or recession could produce a rally. The trade's attractiveness depends on the distribution of those moves relative to the insurance price.

The current rate is neither the much lower pre-tightening level nor a later peak. Assessing expected return requires acknowledging that material repricing has already occurred. Historical cheap-insurance successes do not prove that today's protection is equally cheap.
docs.D03_treasury_supply.md:
Title: Borrowing requirements, refunding and a sovereign downgrade
Source: compiled from: https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy1662; https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy1671; https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/fitch-cuts-us-governments-aaa-credit-rating-by-one-notch-2023-08-01
Date: 2023-08-02

On July 31, Treasury projected $1.007 trillion privately held net marketable borrowing in July-September, assuming a $650 billion end-September cash balance. The estimate was $274 billion above the May projection.

Treasury attributed the increase primarily to a lower beginning cash balance, a higher assumed ending cash balance and fiscal-flow changes. A cash-balance rebuild is not the same as a permanent increase in annual deficits, and those components should not be conflated.

The same announcement projected $852 billion borrowing for October-December with a $750 billion ending cash balance. These are financing estimates, not completed issuance or a forecast of which maturity investors will absorb at a given yield.

The August 2 refunding statement offers $103 billion securities to refinance approximately $84 billion maturing August 15, raising about $19 billion new cash. The securities are $42 billion three-year notes, $38 billion ten-year notes and $23 billion thirty-year bonds.

The distinction between gross issuance, refunding and net new cash is important. Calling all $103 billion incremental deficit financing would overstate the immediate new funding requirement.

Greater duration supply can require higher yields if demand does not rise comparably. However, auction composition, cash-management choices, private demand, regulatory demand and broader macro conditions affect the outcome. Supply alone does not determine a fair 30-year yield.

Fitch downgraded the United States from AAA to AA+ on August 1. Reuters reports concerns about fiscal deterioration and repeated debt-ceiling confrontations; Treasury criticized the decision as arbitrary.

The downgrade provides a fiscal/governance risk signal. It does not establish imminent default, a particular change in institutional mandates or a quantified forced-sale flow. No such mechanism is asserted without evidence.

For a duration hedge, the supply/downgrade backdrop can strengthen a term-premium risk scenario. The countercase is that weaker growth, disinflation or safe-haven demand more than offsets new supply.

All facts in this document were public by August 2. Later auction outcomes, yield peaks and geopolitical shocks are excluded, leaving the genuine underwriting question of whether these financing pressures are inadequately reflected in current long-rate pricing.
docs.D04_instrument_economics.md:
Title: Bond shorts and payer options are different trades
Source: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2023/03/29160536/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-2022-Annual-Report.pdf
Date: 2023-03-29

The manager's already published 2022 annual report defines swaptions and discloses US and Japanese interest-rate option exposure. A swaption gives its owner a right, not an obligation, to enter or cancel a specified swap on a future date under agreed terms.

A payer swaption generally benefits when the relevant fixed swap rate rises relative to its strike. Its economics differ from selling a Treasury security outright. It has an option premium, expiry, underlying tenor and volatility exposure, not just linear bond duration.

An outright short bond position gains when bond prices fall but can suffer losses from a rally, financing/borrow costs and coupon payments. Losses are not inherently capped at an initial option premium.

A purchased option can define the upfront premium at risk, subject to its actual terms and any separate financing arrangements. That potential convexity is attractive for insurance, but time decay, expensive implied volatility and wrong maturity/strike can make a correct macro view unprofitable.

Swap rates and Treasury yields can diverge. A payer swaption on a long swap is not identical to an option on a particular Treasury bond. The hedge therefore includes basis risk alongside the broad interest-rate direction.

The annual report's year-end risk table gives a US thirty-year option fair value of approximately $330.722 million. That is a historical mark, not original cost, notional, premium budget or a verified August 2 valuation.

The report's rate-shock sensitivities demonstrate nonlinearity, but they are model-based year-end disclosures. They cannot be treated as August dealer quotes or a guarantee that the same gains/losses occur after time and market conditions change.

No current contract-level strike, expiry, notional, premium or implied volatility was recovered. The pack therefore cannot establish a precise five-to-tenfold payoff or a specific percent-NAV cost. An analyst should request those terms rather than infer them from a yield forecast.

The decision is not merely “will long yields rise?” It is whether the chosen structure pays usefully in the portfolio's adverse scenario, has an affordable carry and can be monetized when its expected protection value changes. Existing gains, if any, are capital at risk too.
docs.D05_portfolio_context.md:
Title: Concentrated equity duration and already disclosed protection
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2023/07/03175656/Performance-Report-June-2023-PSH.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2023/03/29160536/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-2022-Annual-Report.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2023/02/09104816/2023-Annual-Investor-Presentation.pdf
Date: 2023-07-03

The June 30 update reports ten long issuer positions, no issuer shorts and 116% net issuer equity/debt exposure. Direct/indirect hedges, cash and expense items are excluded from those counts and exposures. “No shorts” in this table therefore does not prove no macro protection.

PSH AUM was $13.081 billion, core strategy AUM $14.9766 billion and total firm AUM including UMG co-investment vehicles $16.1545 billion. The footnotes add back $1.8 billion and €500 million bond principal and do not deduct accrued performance fees.

These are not interchangeable with equity NAV or dry powder. A premium expressed as a fraction of gross AUM can understate its size relative to shareholder capital. Co-investment capital is also not unrestricted cash for every vehicle.

PSH returned 10.0% net and 10.9% gross through June. Those performance figures are not current position weights or proof that the portfolio has little downside.

The February presentation and annual report describe concentrated franchise ownership, including consumer, hospitality, media, retail, transport and real-estate exposures. Businesses with durable future earnings can still be sensitive to discount rates through valuation and financing channels.

The March annual report already discloses long-rate option protection. The August decision is therefore not clean first inception. It can be interpreted as whether to retain, add, reshape or close protection given current yields and option value.

The hedge may serve a portfolio purpose even when a standalone trader would have monetized an earlier gain. Conversely, retaining protection has opportunity cost and can lose value if rates fall or time passes.

Exact August equity weights, aggregate portfolio duration, cash, current option terms and contract-level P&L were not recovered. No mechanically optimal hedge ratio is derived.

The relevant portfolio test is whether long-rate stress materially harms expected equity value and whether the option payoff supplies useful offsetting liquidity at an affordable cost. A broad macro narrative does not establish that match, and the fund's previous hedge successes should not substitute for underwriting the present structure.
docs.D06_risks_alternatives.md:
Title: Bond-supportive evidence and alternatives to a long-rate overlay
Source: compiled from: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_07122023.pdf; https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20230726a.htm; https://www.bea.gov/sites/default/files/2023-07/gdp2q23_adv.pdf; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/DGS30
Date: 2023-08-02

The bond-supportive case starts with disinflation. June CPI was 3.0% headline and 4.8% core, with both monthly measures up 0.2%. A continuation of lower monthly inflation could reduce the compensation investors require to hold long-duration nominal bonds.

The Federal Reserve has tightened materially and emphasizes cumulative policy effects and lags. The July GDP estimate remains positive, but it does not rule out a future slowdown. Long yields can decline before contemporaneous activity becomes visibly weak.

Safe-haven demand is another general risk to a bond short. Unexpected stress can lower long yields even when deficits are large. No specific future conflict or market event is used as a known catalyst.

The observed 30-year yield has already risen to 4.17%. The expected payoff from further increases should be assessed from that level and current option pricing, not from an earlier low-yield entry remembered from a past trade.

A long-rate payer option can lose through falling rates, time decay or changes in volatility. A direct Treasury short adds financing, coupon and uncapped rally risks. Wrong tenor/strike and swap-Treasury basis can impair protection even if a broad inflation concern is justified.

Alternatives include reducing long-equity duration, increasing cash, paying down leverage, buying equity puts or accepting some exposure. Each has different taxes, opportunity costs, carry and basis risk.

The comparison should use common scenarios: sustained disinflation/soft landing, persistent inflation with high real rates, recession and risk-off stress. Evaluate the portfolio and hedge together rather than optimize a standalone yield target.

No authentic current quote set for those alternatives was recovered, so no numerical cost ranking is invented. Nor is there evidence that the investor must preserve every existing hedge regardless of price.

Useful falsifiers include durable core disinflation, weaker forward activity, materially improved long-bond compensation or an option premium too expensive relative to remaining stress payoff. Position changes should respond to those facts, not to the desire to validate a public macro thesis.

The trade is an insurance/expected-return decision under uncertainty. Persistent deficits and inflation risk can coexist with a near-term bond rally; a responsible overlay must be sized to survive that possibility.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: Information sequence through August 2
Source: compiled from: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20230726a.htm; https://www.bea.gov/sites/default/files/2023-07/gdp2q23_adv.pdf; https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy1662; https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy1671; https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/fitch-cuts-us-governments-aaa-credit-rating-by-one-notch-2023-08-01
Date: 2023-08-02

**March 29:** The manager's 2022 annual report publicly documents interest-rate option protection and year-end sensitivity data. This establishes that the later public long-rate thesis is not necessarily an August initiation.

**July 3:** The June month-end portfolio update reports 116% net issuer exposure and AUM definitions that include PSH debt. Its zero issuer shorts do not include all hedge categories.

**July 12:** June CPI is released, showing substantial headline disinflation and lower monthly core inflation while year-over-year core remains elevated. Later inflation releases are not yet available.

**July 26:** The Fed raises its target range to 5.25%-5.50% and retains a data-dependent stance. It notes inflation remains elevated and recognizes the role of cumulative tightening and policy lags.

**July 27:** The advance Q2 GDP estimate is 2.4% annualized. This is the then-current release vintage; later revisions must not replace it in the decision set.

**July 28:** The June personal-income/outlays release adds further disinflation evidence, with core PCE still above the Fed objective.

**July 31:** Treasury raises its July-September net marketable borrowing estimate to $1.007 trillion, reflecting cash-balance and fiscal-flow assumptions. The 30-year benchmark yield is 4.02%.

**August 1:** Fitch downgrades US sovereign credit to AA+ from AAA. Treasury disputes the decision. The 30-year benchmark yield is 4.11%.

**August 2:** Treasury announces a $103 billion refunding package with $19 billion approximate new cash. Daily H.15 yields are 4.08% at ten years and 4.17% at thirty years.

The pack permits end-of-day information and does not claim those yields were executable before their measurement. The manager's same-day directional social-media statement is withheld to avoid giving the decision label; the later Reuters report verifying it belongs in the key.

No October peak, realized cover, later war or subsequent economic evidence appears here. The test is a contemporaneous decision about an existing protection overlay with incomplete contract terms, not a hindsight exercise that starts at the known low and ends at the known high.

drivers.driver: Structural inflation nearer3% than2% could justify materially higher long yields, around5.5% in the public framework.
Large deficits and Treasury supply add long-rate/term-premium pressure.
Protect equity duration while taking an attractive standalone asymmetric exposure.
drivers.quote: We are short in size the 30-year T.

drivers.driver: Retained payer swaptions as portfolio insurance rather than simply an outright linear cash-bond short.

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: Seven hedge-specific documents. Authentic vintage macro/supply/curve and pre-existing public option disclosure. Not a clean new inception; score maintain/add/cover interpretation. No current option surface/strike/premium/notional, no forced 5-10x claim. Direct X scrape unavailable; Reuters verifies original statement and date.

final.risk: Structural inflation and higher-for-longer term premiums on long-duration sovereign debt, exacerbated by increased Treasury supply [D03].
final.market_implied_probability: Implied by the rise in 30-year yields to 4.17% [D02] and recent fiscal downgrade [D03].
final.our_probability_and_why: Moderate-to-high. While disinflation is occurring, the scale of Treasury issuance and the risk of structural inflation suggest that the bond market has not fully priced the long-term term premium [D01], [D03].
final.instrument: Payer swaptions on long-term interest rates [D04].
final.exit_rule: Exit when the asymmetry is resolved, either through realized rate increases hitting our target or a meaningful shift in the fiscal/inflation paradigm that removes the tail-risk protection requirement [D06].

drivers.driver: Persistently elevated core inflation requires a term-premium risk adjustment not yet fully reflected in long-bond yields.
Increased Treasury net marketable borrowing supply creates technical pressure on long-duration yields.
Existing option protection provides essential tail-risk coverage for our concentrated equity positions at an established cost.

final.memo:
Our portfolio remains concentrated in high-quality, free-cash-flow-generative businesses that are generally durable, but we remain mindful of the sensitivity of long-duration assets to discount rate volatility [D05]. The current macro environment exhibits a tug-of-war between observed disinflation and the structural risks of significant fiscal deficits and increased Treasury issuance [D01], [D03].

Given that we have already deployed capital into long-rate payer swaptions to protect against the paradigm-shifting risk of inflation and term-premium expansion, we view this as a decision to maintain our hedge [D04], [D05]. We do not believe the market has adequately compensated for the fiscal outlook or the potential for long-term yields to remain higher than historical averages [D02]. We continue to hold our existing protection to ensure our portfolio is resilient against a sharp, disorderly move in the long end of the curve, rather than attempting to trade the interim noise [D06].

final.risk: Structural inflation and increasing term premium resulting from sustained federal fiscal deficits and supply-demand imbalances in the long-end Treasury market [D03].
final.market_implied_probability: Market pricing for 30-year Treasuries implies a yield of 4.17%, reflecting normalization and term compensation expectations rather than a terminal policy rate [D02].
final.our_probability_and_why: Moderate-to-high. While disinflation is evident in June CPI and PCE data [D01], the significant increase in projected Treasury borrowing requirements [D03] and the sovereign credit downgrade [D03] create a risk of higher long-term yields if supply outpaces demand, justifying the maintenance of existing insurance [D05].
final.exit_rule: Exit when term premium is appropriately priced by the market or if inflation expectations durably anchor to the Fed's 2% objective, reducing the asymmetric risk of a long-bond sell-off [D06].

drivers.driver: Treasury's increased borrowing requirements and the Fitch downgrade highlight fiscal pressures that may necessitate higher term premiums [D03].
Existing interest-rate options provide cost-effective protection against a nonlinear rise in long-end rates [D04].
The portfolio maintains high net equity exposure, necessitating continued macro hedging to mitigate potential volatility from discount rate adjustments [D05].

final.memo:
We remain positioned with our interest-rate protection as of August 2, 2023. While we observe clear disinflationary trends in the most recent CPI and PCE releases [D01], the broader fiscal landscape—characterized by significantly increased Treasury borrowing estimates and a sovereign credit rating downgrade [D03]—suggests that the market may be underestimating the term premium required to absorb the duration supply hitting the market [D03].

Our current hedge, established previously [D05], serves as essential insurance for our concentrated equity portfolio. Given the current 30-year yield of 4.17% [D02], we believe the risk of an upward repricing due to fiscal and supply-side factors remains significant [D03]. Maintaining this overlay offers us necessary protection against interest-rate shocks without requiring us to take an outright directional short position, which would introduce uncapped risks and financing costs [D04].

We continue to monitor for durable evidence of disinflation and cooling economic activity [D06]. Until such time as these trends suggest a permanent shift in long-term inflation expectations, the asymmetry of our existing interest-rate options remains favorable [D06]. We are not adding to or trimming the position, opting instead to hold our protection as a prudent buffer in a period of fiscal uncertainty [D05].
uncited_claims: The hedge serves a portfolio purpose even when a standalone trader would have monetized an earlier gain.
